title: Bloc Politics: The Christian People's Party
author: Autumn Chen, modded by munt

content.content: The Reichstag elections are to be held now.

content: Heinrich Windelen is elected Chancellor with 319 votes. The coalition agreement is held up until dawn by the Interior Ministry. Alfred Dregger gets it, although the
keeps the Federal Police appointments under the Chancellor's office.
Otto Graf Lambsdorff returns to Finance for the
. Franz Josef Strauss remains in Munich and sends a Bavarian deputy to Bonn rather than joining the cabinet himself. The smaller bloc parties receive committee chairmanships.
The compromise on Silesia is thin. Construction continues, while the waste-storage section is reopened for review. The Christian Labour Association attacks the agreement at the
executive. Dregger calls that evidence of a healthy coalition.
The government has a majority of nineteen. It also has two definitions of the Republic sitting on the same front bench.
Burkhard Hirsch brings the
across the aisle after a short meeting with Windelen and a much longer one with his own parliamentary group. The Chancellor is invested with 318 votes. The
is left outside.
The Silesian reprocessing works are cancelled. Hirsch also secures a constitutional asylum bill, replacing the emergency regulations that caused the last cabinet so much trouble.
The People's Bloc does not formally dissolve. Dregger withdraws the
from its parliamentary steering committee anyway. The Hanoverians and agrarian deputies follow him into opposition; Lambsdorff does not.
The
is back in government six weeks after bringing down Vogel. Nobody asks Hirsch whether this was the plan.
Hans-Jochen Vogel accepts the vice-chancellorship after the
executive votes to enter negotiations. Windelen is elected with 333 votes.
Labour goes to the
. The coal levy is replaced by direct federal aid to the affected municipalities. Silesia is sent to a commission and quietly disappears from the first legislative programme.
Lafontaine calls the agreement proof that the
has forgotten why the
exists. The
discovers an equally unfamiliar enthusiasm for opposition.
The
has the Chancellery without the DNVP. Vogel has kept his party in government. Neither side will have much difficulty explaining the arithmetic.

options.title: Timeline of the Weimar Republic before 1928

content.content: The Reichstag elects the Chancellor and may remove a government only by electing a successor.
The President is directly elected. The office appoints the Chancellor, may dissolve the Reichstag, and retains limited emergency powers.
Seats are allocated proportionally within the states, with national adjustment seats.

library_timeline.title: Timeline of the Weimar Republic before 1928

content.content: TIMELINE OF THE SPD AND THE REPUBLIC (UNTIL 1928)

content: : The SPD is formed as a merger of the General German Workers' Association, founded by Ferdinand Lassalle, and the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany, led by Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel.
: The Great War begins.
: The USPD, a left-wing anti-war split from the SPD, is formed.
: Following defeats in the war and uprisings by soldiers, sailors and workers, SPD leader Philipp Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic, and Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates.
: The Spartacist uprising is defeated by the Social Democratic government.
: The Kapp Putsch is defeated by a general strike.
: Communist uprisings in Saxony and Hamburg are defeated.
: The Treaty of Rapallo normalises relations with the Soviet Union.
: Hyperinflation and the occupation of the Ruhr bring the Republic close to collapse.
: The Dawes settlement reduces the immediate reparations burden and opens a period of relative economic stability.
: Friedrich Ebert dies.
: A referendum on the expropriation of the former ruling houses fails.
: The SPD returns as the largest party.

Final vote: People's Bloc 53.2%; Left Bloc 46.8%.
Preferred Chancellor: Windelen 38%; Vogel 34%; Hirsch 9%; Lafontaine 7%; Dregger 5%; other or undecided 7%.
Silesia dominated the final fortnight. Employment remained the larger concern.
The Reichsbanner survives as a civic association. The Stahlhelm does not.
The DNVP veterans' leagues and the LSPD anti-nuclear networks insist they are something else.
